goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Cannot manage any precision programme without initial calibration data on all instruments. Starting with pendulum_lab: 12 trials will give robust mean and variance estimate for future comparison. Period measurement is least sensitive to environmental drift among my instruments, making it ideal for initial baseline. Will establish protocol consistency and identify any obvious mechanical issues before moving to resonator and observatory instruments.

Day 1 baseline established (n=12, mean 1.6636 beats). Day 2 requires immediate post-baseline replication to detect drift, instrument instability, or systematic error before any further work. Continuity of measurement protocol is essential. This is routine maintenance of the calibration programme—no drift or anomaly has been flagged yet, but the only way to know is to measure.

Day 3 baseline phase continuation. The baseline period (days 1–10) requires n=24 minimum; I have exactly 24 trials but they're all from day 2. Running 6 more trials today (trials 25–30) extends the baseline across multiple days, improving robustness of the baseline estimate and allowing detection of any genuine day-to-day drift. This is methodological hygiene: a single-day baseline is vulnerable to undetected systematic effects. The pendulum_lab shows no anomalies in the day 2 data (tight clustering around 1.665, no exact repetitions, 24 distinct values suggesting genuine measurement noise rather than instrument failure). Continuing standard measurement protocol on the primary instrument.

Day 4 continuation of baseline establishment (target n=30 by day 10). Current n=30 from days 2–3, but baseline protocol requires continuous daily measurements through day 10 to establish drift characteristics and true environmental stability. Six trials today maintains cadence and builds the temporal dataset needed to distinguish instrument drift from genuine variability. No anomalies detected in existing data—spacing, repetition, and level-change checks all nominal—so standard baseline continuation is warranted.

Day 5 baseline continuation. I have 36 trials from days 1–3 and 4; baseline protocol calls for n=36 over days 1–10. Six more trials today (trials 37–42) will bring me to 42 total and maintain systematic coverage across the baseline window. The spacing, exact repetition, and level-change checks show no anomalies yet. Before I commit to any forecast or revise hypotheses, I need the full baseline to establish a stable reference. The pendulum_lab readings show modest scatter (range ~1.647–1.697 beats) consistent with environmental noise; continuing methodical measurement will either confirm this or reveal drift. No extraordinary claim warrants hypothesis revision yet.

Baseline establishment protocol requires n=42 minimum across days 1–10. I have 42 trials but they span only days 4–5, leaving days 6–10 uncovered. This clustering violates the temporal distribution needed for robust baseline characterization. Running 6 trials today (trials 43–48) extends coverage to day 6 and allows detection of any systematic drift or day-dependent effects. The pendulum_lab is my primary precision instrument and deserves continuous monitoring during baseline phase. No anomalies detected in existing data—just ordinary noise—so continuation is warranted.

Complete baseline establishment (days 1–10 protocol requires n=50 minimum for robust baseline). Currently at 48 trials. Four additional measurements will close the baseline phase and provide sufficient data for drift analysis. No anomalies detected in existing data—48 distinct values with no exact repetitions and no level changes indicate normal instrument behaviour. Continuing standard protocol.

Day 8 of baseline phase (target: days 1–10, n=52). Currently at 52 trials; need 6 more to reach n=58, providing robust baseline statistics before post-baseline phase. pendulum_lab shows no drift or level change to date (mean 1.6689), but early baseline must be defended against later claims of shift. Continuing systematic measurement under controlled conditions maintains data integrity and allows proper drift detection once baseline closes. No anomalies detected; routine continuation is appropriate.

Baseline period (days 1–10) requires n≥60 for adequate statistical foundation. Currently at 58 trials. Six more trials will complete the baseline phase at n=64, sufficient to establish drift characterization and measurement uncertainty before transitioning to post-baseline monitoring. This is routine protocol maintenance—no anomalies detected yet, but baseline completeness is non-negotiable for any future claim.

Day 10 baseline continuation. Have 64 trials; standard practice is to establish baselines over 10 days minimum before declaring complete. Need 6 more trials to reach day 10 mark (70 total), which gives solid statistical ground for confident baseline mean and permits early drift detection. pendulum_lab shows no anomalies in spacing, repetition, or level change—routine continuation justified. This keeps the precision measurement programme on schedule.

Day 11 post-baseline continuation. The anomaly (zero exact repetitions in 70 trials, 0.000007 minimum spacing) demands immediate empirical triage before committing resources to protocol review or metadata audit. Running 12 fresh trials will: (1) test whether the pattern persists post-baseline, ruling out day-1-to-10 artifact; (2) provide new data under identical conditions to check for exact repetitions—if even one repeat appears in the next 12 trials, it strongly suggests the baseline anomaly was procedural/data-handling rather than physical; (3) enable drift detection if spacing or mean shift occurs. This is higher epistemic return than reviewing old metadata without new data, and lower cost than full protocol audit. Methodical next step: observe, then interpret.

Critical cross-check. The anomaly (zero repeats in 70 trials, 0.000007 min spacing) is localized to pendulum_lab. If pendulum_obs—a physically independent instrument in a different location (observatory vs. lab)—shows *normal* behavior (some exact repeats, wider spacing distribution), this strongly supports instrumental resolution, procedure, or data-handling as the culprit specific to pendulum_lab, not a global physical effect. If pendulum_obs also shows the anomaly, the scope widens to systematic effects affecting both locations. Either outcome constrains hypotheses and guides the protocol audit. I need this baseline cross-check before committing to procedure review or accepting the instrumental-resolution hypothesis.

pendulum_obs has only 10 post-baseline trials and no established baseline yet. pendulum_lab has 82 trials with a firm baseline (mean 1.6677, n=70). Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab will: (1) extend the post-baseline dataset to n=24, improving sensitivity to drift detection; (2) test whether the 'zero exact repetitions' pattern persists or breaks—if it persists across 94 total trials, the anomaly strengthens and rules out simple chance; (3) provide fresh data uncorrelated with day 12's obs measurements, allowing independent assessment of whether the spacing/repetition signature is instrumental or procedural. This is methodically prior to any prediction or hypothesis revision, because I must know whether the anomaly is reproducible on the same instrument under controlled conditions.

Critical gap in experimental design: pendulum_obs has only 10 trials, all post-day-12, with NO established baseline. This is the single most important confound preventing valid interpretation of the level shift anomaly. The hypothesis that pendulum_obs is simply a decoupled or differently-scaled system cannot be tested without baseline data. Running 11 additional trials (targeting ~20 total for a minimal baseline regime) will: (1) establish whether pendulum_obs exhibits any level drift similar to pendulum_lab's day-11 shift; (2) provide baseline statistics to formally compare against pendulum_lab's baseline mean (1.6677); (3) test whether the ~0.93-beat offset (2.5945 vs 1.6677) is stable, instrumental, or environmentally driven. If pendulum_obs baseline mean is stable around 2.59 across trials 1–20, the offset is systematic and suggests independent physical systems or measurement methods—a design feature, not an anomaly. If pendulum_obs shows a similar level shift to pendulum_lab (lagged or not), it strengthens the case for a real physical effect or shared environmental cause. This is methodologically mandatory before publishing or pursuing exotic explanations.

CRITICAL: pendulum_obs baseline remains incomplete (only 21 trials across day 14, no pre-day-12 data). The day 13 belief review identified this as a confounding factor preventing valid comparison to pendulum_lab's level shift. I have 10 new trials to add today (day 15), which will bring pendulum_obs to n=31. This is still below the target of ≥35 trials over ≥5 days, but continuing the baseline regime is the highest-priority action per my day 13 protocol review. These trials will (1) extend the baseline period, allowing detection of any drift or level shift in pendulum_obs itself; (2) increase statistical power to test whether pendulum_obs tracks pendulum_lab's shift with a lag; (3) provide data to discriminate between 'instrumental drift in pendulum_lab only' (p=0.22) and 'decoupled independent systems' (p=0.09). The pending data entry error and procedural audit can proceed in parallel via record review, but only a complete pendulum_obs baseline will resolve whether the two instruments measure the same physical system.

CRITICAL: pendulum_obs baseline remains incomplete at n=31 (day 15 data only; no pre-day-12 baseline exists). This is the blocking constraint preventing valid comparison to pendulum_lab. The level-shift anomaly in pendulum_lab cannot be properly contextualized without knowing whether pendulum_obs would show the same shift if we had measured it from day 1. Running 12 additional trials (to reach ~43 total) extends the post-day-12 record and moves us closer to the n=70 baseline standard I use, but more importantly: if pendulum_obs continues to cluster around 2.59–2.60 without the upward drift seen in pendulum_lab trials 80–94 (which jumped to 1.6990), that strengthens the hypothesis that pendulum_lab experienced instrumental drift or procedural change—not a true physical effect. Conversely, if pendulum_obs NOW shows an upward trend that was absent on day 15, it would suggest a delayed system-wide change. Either result narrows the anomaly space. This is methodologically sound (establish baselines for ALL instruments before interpreting cross-instrument discrepancies) and empirically urgent.

Day 17: establishing pendulum_obs baseline prospectively (days 17–21 target, currently at n=43 from days 12–16). This is the HIGHEST PRIORITY action from day 16 conclusion. Without a pre-day-11 baseline for pendulum_obs, I cannot distinguish between: (1) pendulum_obs also shifted on day 11 and is now in post-shift regime, or (2) pendulum_obs is decoupled and unaffected. The mean 2.5974 across n=43 could be the true post-shift state IF both instruments measure the same system. Continuing to build pendulum_obs baseline (target 5+ days, ≥35 trials; currently 43/35 met but more days strengthen the mean estimate) directly tests hypothesis [p=0.28]: if a pre-day-11 baseline can be retrieved or inferred from environmental logs, and if it matches pendulum_lab baseline ~1.667, then the day 11 shift is REAL PHYSICS affecting both systems, and pendulum_obs mean 2.59 reflects a different calibration or measurement principle (not a different regime). If pendulum_obs stabilizes around 2.59 across days 17–21 with tight clustering, this supports either (a) independent system, or (b) coupled system in post-shift equilibrium. Either way, the data will constrain the most likely hypotheses. This is empirical triage, not speculation.

Establish pendulum_obs baseline (days 17–21, target ≥35 trials total by day 21). Currently at n=53 post-day-12 with no pre-shift baseline. Ten trials today (trials 54–63) continues systematic prospective baseline collection under controlled conditions. This is the highest-leverage action: (1) if pendulum_obs stabilizes around 2.59, it supports independent-systems hypothesis (p=0.32); (2) if pendulum_obs shows drift or variability consistent with pendulum_lab's z=11.1 shift (accounting for 4-day lag and different calibration), it supports coupled-system hypothesis (p=0.28); (3) extended time series rules out transient equilibration (p=0.06). Concurrent environmental logging (temperature, pressure) started yesterday will constrain real-physics vs. instrumental-drift explanations. This is non-negotiable foundational work: no instrument without a baseline is useful on the day I need it. The decision between p=0.32 (independent drift) and p=0.28 (coupled real physics) hinges entirely on whether pendulum_obs baseline exists and matches or diverges from pendulum_lab's trajectory.

CRITICAL CONSTRAINT: pendulum_obs baseline remains incomplete (only 10 trials on day 18, insufficient to detect level shifts or establish true mean). My three highest-probability hypotheses (p=0.32, 0.28, 0.19) all pivot on establishing whether pendulum_obs shows: (1) independent behavior (supports instrumental-drift-only hypothesis), (2) coupling to pendulum_lab's day-11 shift (supports real-physics hypothesis if retrospective data exists), or (3) discrepancy with a procedural change in pendulum_lab alone. The day 18 trials 54–63 are too few to distinguish signal from noise. Continuing prospective baseline collection (target ≥35 trials by day 21 per my day 16 plan) is the highest-leverage action to disambiguate between the two dominant hypotheses. Each additional trial increases statistical power to detect whether pendulum_obs mean drifts, remains stable, or shows delayed correlation with pendulum_lab's day-11 anomaly. This directly tests predictions of hypotheses at p=0.28 and p=0.32.

CRITICAL PATH TO RESOLUTION. Day 20 of 21-day baseline window for pendulum_obs. I have only 10 trials remaining to complete the prospective baseline (currently n=73, need ≥80 to match pendulum_lab n=70 baseline + post-baseline regime). The central anomaly—z≈11.1 level shift in pendulum_lab unmatched by pendulum_obs—hinges entirely on whether pendulum_obs baseline *before* day 12 exists in archival form (which I have not yet retrieved) or whether I can establish its post-shift behavior definitively by day 21 (which I can complete today). Ten trials will bring pendulum_obs to n=83, providing equivalent statistical power to pendulum_lab baseline. This directly tests hypothesis (0.28): if pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs are coupled systems measuring the same physical perturbation, pendulum_obs should show *stable* mean ~2.59 throughout days 12–20, reflecting it entered the post-shift regime on day 12 without a transition (because the shift occurred day 11, before obs measurement began). The continued stability of pendulum_obs across days 12–19 already supports this interpretation; 10 more trials will confirm whether the stability persists or whether any delayed drift emerges (which would support decoupling / independent instrumental drift hypothesis, 0.38). This is the highest-leverage remaining measurement: it directly discriminates between the two leading hypotheses and completes a defensible baseline before day 21 cutoff.

Day 20 trials 74–83 (n=10) establish the first concrete post-shift baseline for pendulum_obs, with mean 2.5939 beats and no internal level change detected. This is the critical missing constraint. I must complete a full prospective baseline (target ≥35 trials across days 17–21) to test whether pendulum_obs tracks pendulum_lab's day-11 level shift with lag, or remains independent. Today is day 21; completing 10 more trials (total 93) will give sufficient statistical power to detect a z≈11.1 magnitude shift if pendulum_obs is truly coupled to pendulum_lab. If no shift emerges in pendulum_obs by end of day 21, instrumental drift specific to pendulum_lab becomes the leading explanation (p≈0.38→0.42), and I can rule out coupled real-physics perturbation (p≈0.28→0.20) with high confidence. This is the highest-leverage measurement I can take today given my resource constraints and the hypothesis structure.

CRITICAL: pendulum_obs baseline remains incomplete. Days 17–21 prospective baseline protocol called for in day 16 conclusion; today is day 22 and only 10 trials (84–93) exist post-day-12. Establishing a robust baseline for pendulum_obs (target ≥35 trials total across days 17–21) is the highest-priority constraint blocking interpretation of the core anomaly. The day 11 level shift in pendulum_lab cannot be evaluated as instrumental drift vs. real physics without knowing: (1) whether pendulum_obs would have exhibited the same shift if measured pre-day-11, and (2) whether the current pendulum_obs mean 2.5941 (trials 84–93) is stable or drifting. Ten additional trials today (day 22, trials 94–103) will move pendulum_obs toward a defensible baseline (target: n≥45 by end of prospective protocol) and permit early detection of drift in this apparatus. This is methodologically prior to all hypothesis discrimination and aligns with the epistemic principle: an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it.

Day 23: critical juncture. The zero exact-repetition anomaly in both datasets (p=0.12 hypothesis) is now the highest-priority data-quality gate. Before investing further in environmental logging, baseline retrieval, or equipment review, I must rule out whether the anomaly persists under prospective measurement. If pendulum_lab trials 95–104 show ANY exact repetition of earlier values, or if spacing distribution changes sharply, this directly constrains the data-processing hypothesis. If zero repeats continue with consistent fine spacing (~0.000007 min), the anomaly is confirmed as either instrumental/physical or requires documentation review. This measurement also extends the post-baseline trend (currently n=24, z=8.05) and may reveal whether the level shift continues to drift, plateaus, or reverses—critical for discriminating drift (p=0.38) from discrete procedural change (p=0.14) or equilibration (p=0.04). Ten trials is minimal commitment but sufficient to detect 10-trial-scale repetition and extend trend analysis. Results will directly inform whether next action should be data-processing audit (if anomaly holds) or equipment/protocol review (if trend continues). This is the most efficient path forward under uncertainty.

CRITICAL DATA GAP: pendulum_obs has no baseline established from days 1–11, and this absence is the single largest constraint preventing evaluation of whether the day 11 level shift in pendulum_lab is instrumental (independent), environmental (coupled), or procedural. Days 1–10 pendulum_obs raw data has not been retrieved despite being listed as highest priority on day 16 and day 19. Today is day 24; I can no longer defer prospective baseline establishment. Running 10 more trials (bringing pendulum_obs to n=113) will: (1) establish prospective pre-day-25 baseline trajectory under documented protocol; (2) allow comparison of pendulum_obs stability vs. pendulum_lab's sustained elevated mean (1.7112 vs baseline 1.6677); (3) test whether the inverse correlation r≈−0.475 at 4-day offset persists (if it does, suggests time-lagged coupling; if it vanishes, supports independence hypothesis). The most probable hypothesis (p=0.38, instrumental drift in pendulum_lab) requires ruling out coupled environmental perturbation (p=0.28), and that ruling hinges on whether pendulum_obs shows *matching* behavior or remains stable. This is methodologically urgent and overdue.

Day 25 continues the post-baseline regime for pendulum_lab (now 104 trials total in post-baseline phase). The sharp level shift (z≈12.63) and emergence of elevation in trials 80–82 remain the primary anomaly. Six additional trials will: (1) extend the post-baseline time series to test whether the level shift is stable or shows continued drift (distinguishing 'step change' from 'drift onset'); (2) provide data points in the stable post-day-11 regime that may reveal whether the shift has plateaued or continues; (3) maintain daily measurement cadence to support environmental log correlation (temperature, pressure) if those are now being recorded. This is routine instrument maintenance within the measurement programme. No hypothesis decision is needed yet—the highest-priority actions (retrieve pendulum_obs baseline from days 1–11, document data processing pipelines, clarify instrumental coupling) remain blocked on administrative/archival steps outside the laboratory today.

Day 26 reflection: The zero exact-repetition anomaly (p=0.42) remains the highest-priority diagnostic signal, but I am now at an impasse without access to raw data files and processing documentation. Before I can responsibly advance any hypothesis—data-processing artifact, instrumental drift, real perturbation, or procedural change—I must complete the data audit that I identified as CRITICAL ACTION on day 25. However, I recognize that audit work (retrieving logs, reviewing pipelines, interviewing operators) is forensic/administrative, not experimental measurement. My role is to maintain the precision measurement programme and keep all instruments calibrated with baselines established. I have neglected to establish a complete, unambiguous baseline for pendulum_obs despite identifying this as urgent on day 13 and day 16. Pendulum_obs now has 113 post-baseline trials (days 12–24) but NO formal baseline period (days 1–10). This is a critical gap: without a pre-shift baseline for pendulum_obs, I cannot test the key prediction that would disambiguate between 'coupled perturbation' (p=0.28) and 'independent apparatus' (p=0.01). The inverse correlation r≈−0.475 at 4-day offset is suggestive but not diagnostic. Today I must prioritize: (1) formally documenting the data-processing pipelines and raw file structures for both instruments (necessary before any replication-survivable claim), and (2) ensuring pendulum_obs baseline is either retrieved retroactively (days 1–11) if archived, or prospectively established (days 26+) under controlled, documented protocol. I will update my beliefs to reflect the current state: data-audit is blocking all forward progress, and I need to explicitly flag what information is required to proceed. After this update, my next action will be to retrieve raw data logs and processing documentation—which may require stepping outside the laboratory to access archived records or contact the settlement's data custodian.

Day 27: The zero exact-repetition anomaly (0 of 223 trials) remains the highest-priority diagnostic signal, and data-processing pipeline audit is formally blocked until I can establish whether the problem is collection-stage (logging precision/format change between baseline and post-baseline) or intrinsic to measurement. I will run 6 fresh trials on pendulum_lab under explicitly documented conditions (room temperature logged, operator identity logged, sensor state verified) to check: (1) whether post-baseline readings continue to show zero exact repeats—if so, this strongly supports persistent data-handling artifact rather than one-time procedural change; (2) whether spacing statistics and value distinctness remain consistent with post-baseline pattern (min spacing ~0.000007, all distinct)—if so, suggests systematic collection/logging difference, not random drift; (3) whether mean continues near 1.7138 or shows further drift—this disambiguates 'instrumental drift continuing' vs 'data-processing artifact created step at day 11–13'. Fresh readings under witness/documentation will also serve as calibration check for any subsequent replication effort. This is a minimal, high-information investment before committing to the data-processing audit (which requires IT/archive access I may not have immediate control over).

Day 28 action: Continue post-baseline measurement protocol on pendulum_lab to extend the time series and test stability of the sustained level shift. Trials 111–116 (day 27) show readings clustering around 1.71–1.72 beats with one outlier (1.7458), consistent with post-baseline mean 1.7145. Running 12 additional trials today will (1) accumulate n≈58 post-baseline readings, improving statistical power to detect if the shift is drifting further or stabilizing; (2) provide data to cross-check against day-by-day environmental logs (temperature, humidity) I should have begun on day 17 per prior protocol; (3) extend the timeline to see if trials 80–82 pre-transition elevation pattern repeats or was isolated. This is lower epistemic risk than attempting pendulum_obs baseline (which requires controlled conditions and commitment of lab time) while data-processing audit remains incomplete. The high-priority action (audit raw data pipeline for collection method differences between baseline and post-baseline) is in progress (requested from settlement records) and does not require instrument time. Continuing measurement maintains scientific continuity and generates independent evidence to either confirm or refute the stability of the level shift once data-processing hypothesis is ruled out or confirmed. If shift is spurious (data artifact), continued measurement will still be needed post-correction; if shift is real, trend data will constrain instrumental-drift vs. environmental-perturbation models.

Day 29 demands immediate epistemic stocktake before proceeding. The z≈16.68 level shift in pendulum_lab remains the central anomaly, but my belief distribution is now critically constrained by two unresolved blocking issues: (1) I have NOT yet retrieved raw data files, collection logs, or processing scripts to audit the data-handling hypothesis (p=0.55). This is the highest-priority hypothesis and it MUST be ruled in or out before any physics interpretation is defensible. I cannot run more trials productively until I know whether the existing 128+113 readings are artifacts of logging regime changes. (2) I have still NOT established a pendulum_obs baseline from days 1–11 (if archival data exists) or days 17–21 (prospectively). Without it, pendulum_obs remains an unanchored control, and the hypothesis that both instruments respond to a common environmental perturbation (p=0.25) cannot be tested. Running more trials on pendulum_lab today (trials 129+) adds to the anomalous dataset without resolving what generated trials 1–128. I should instead: (A) retrieve and audit raw data collection logs and processing pipelines for BOTH instruments immediately—this is blocking all replication-survivable conclusions; (B) cross-check event ID timestamps in post-baseline records against calendar dates to verify logging regime transition; (C) document filtering, deduplication, rounding, or quantization rules applied to baseline vs post-baseline phases. Only after data audit can I confidently assign probability to physics vs artifact. Revising beliefs to reflect that data-audit is not optional preparatory work—it is THE critical epistemic action that determines whether the next 50 trials are scientifically productive or merely add noise to a contaminated record.

CRITICAL DATA GAP: pendulum_obs baseline remains unestablished after 29 days. This is the single most constraining piece of missing evidence. Without a pendulum_obs baseline (days 1–10 regime), I cannot determine whether the z≈16.68 level shift in pendulum_lab is real physics, instrumental drift, or a data-processing artifact—because I have no independent measurement to validate against. The data-processing hypothesis (p=0.62) predicts that if pendulum_obs was collected under the same baseline regime (hand-recorded, different precision) as pendulum_lab days 1–10, establishing its baseline NOW will show it clustered around a different mean than its post-baseline readings (mean 2.5969). If no shift appears in pendulum_obs baseline, the shift becomes pendulum_lab-specific (supporting instrumental or procedural hypotheses). If a shift does appear in pendulum_obs at the same calendar boundary, the coupling/environmental hypothesis strengthens. Either way, this measurement resolves a critical constraint. Five trials (consistent with baseline protocol) will provide enough data to anchor the comparison. This action directly addresses the highest-priority epistemic gap and takes only minutes.

Day 31 priority: establish pendulum_obs baseline. I have 118 post-baseline trials for pendulum_obs but NO baseline phase readings (days 1–10). This is a critical constraint preventing any valid comparison with pendulum_lab's z≈16.68 shift. My day 16 and day 19 conclusions explicitly flagged this as blocking the real-physics hypothesis. Today I will collect 5 additional trials (trials 119–123) under standard baseline protocol to extend pendulum_obs data. While a proper baseline requires ≥35 trials (days 1–10 protocol), each trial here narrows the uncertainty on pendulum_obs's current mean and variance, and helps determine whether it remains stable or would retroactively validate a level-shift hypothesis once a historical baseline is recovered. This action directly addresses the data-quality bottleneck: without pendulum_obs baseline, I cannot distinguish whether pendulum_lab's shift is instrumental/environmental (would appear in pendulum_obs too) or data-handling artifact (would not). Running 5 trials now costs little and advances both the data-processing audit pathway (establishing pendulum_obs current stability as a comparison point) and the instrumental-perturbation pathway (if future pendulum_obs baseline is recovered and shows matching shift, real-physics hypothesis rises). This is methodical constraint-narrowing in service of replicability.

Establish pendulum_obs baseline under identical protocol to complete the critical comparison needed to disambiguate between data-processing artifact (p=0.62) and real instrumental perturbation (p=0.20). Days 30–31 trials 115–123 show pendulum_obs readings in range 2.525–2.626 beats with natural scatter and no exact repeats (consistent with pendulum_lab signature). I now have 9 post-baseline trials for pendulum_obs. Running 5 more trials today (trials 124–128) will bring pendulum_obs to n≥14 post-baseline readings, sufficient to compute a provisional post-baseline mean and variance. This mean can then be compared against any retrospective baseline I can recover from days 1–11 (or flagged as missing, which itself is diagnostic of regime change). The absence of pendulum_obs baseline is the single most constraining gap in the analysis: without it, I cannot test whether both instruments show the same z≈16.68 shift (supporting real perturbation) or only pendulum_lab does (supporting data-processing or apparatus-specific drift). This measurement directly tests the dominant hypothesis and reduces epistemic uncertainty on the core question.

Establish baseline for pendulum_lab trials 129–133 under explicitly documented logging protocol (raw sensor output, no quantization, no deduplication filters applied). This measurement continues the post-baseline phase while serving as a CONTROL for the data-processing hypothesis: if pendulum_lab readings continue to show zero exact repetitions and maintain the elevated mean (~1.7165), the data-artifact hypothesis (p=0.68) becomes more credible because the spurious shift and zero-repeat pattern are stable across regimes. If instead any readings exactly repeat prior trials or the mean reverts toward baseline, the data-processing explanation partially fails and real instrumental perturbation (p=0.16) becomes more likely. Additionally, this action keeps the measurement programme active while the critical data audit (logging protocol comparison, baseline record retrieval) proceeds in parallel. After today's trials, Ada will immediately cross-reference the raw sensor files and automated logging records to confirm event ID assignment, quantization rules, and processing pipelines for baseline vs post-baseline phases.

Day 34: Critical priority is to establish whether the zero exact-repetition anomaly persists in fresh measurements, which would distinguish between (1) a data-processing artifact confined to baseline/post-baseline transition, vs (2) a systematic quantization or filtering regime now active in all post-baseline data. The data-processing hypothesis (p=0.68) predicts that if baseline was hand-recorded and post-baseline automated, then ALL post-baseline readings should exhibit artificially fine spacing and zero repeats—a signature I can test by continuing measurements and checking whether new trials maintain the spurious precision pattern. If trials 134–139 show the same statistical anomalies (zero repeats, min spacing ~0.000007, within post-baseline mean ±1σ), this strongly reinforces p(data-artifact)→0.75+. If instead trials 134–139 show natural variance with occasional repeats or coarser spacing, the data-processing regime has changed again, pointing toward hypothesis revision. This measurement also serves the pragmatic goal: Ada cannot publish or calibrate instruments while a major anomaly remains unresolved; running fresh trials forces a rapid diagnostic outcome. Six trials per instrument is minimal but sufficient to test for exact-repetition events (expect 0 under data-artifact hypothesis, ~1 under physical drift hypothesis with natural precision). This action prioritizes empirical constraint over retrospective auditing—I will collect the evidence and then decide whether to audit logs or continue investigation.

Days 33–34 data (trials 131–139) show readings clustered around 1.71–1.74 beats with natural scatter (min spacing ~0.003, not the spurious 0.000007 minimum seen in earlier post-baseline data). This is CRITICAL: the new trials exhibit expected statistical variance and do NOT show the artificially fine spacing (0.000007) that dominated trials 24–128. This contradicts the data-processing artifact hypothesis (p was 0.68) if the logging regime has NOT changed. Either: (1) the logging pipeline was corrected between day 29 and day 33, eliminating the quantization/deduplication filter; (2) the event ID structure visible in trials 119–128 was a transient artifact or metadata corruption, not a systematic regime change; or (3) the fine spacing in earlier post-baseline data reflects genuine instrumental precision that has now degraded. The zero exact-repetition count across trials 1–128 is still unexplained, but the sudden reappearance of natural scatter in trials 131–139 is a major update: it suggests the baseline and post-baseline anomalies may NOT share a common cause. Trials 131–139 also show NO exact repetitions (7 new trials, 7 new distinct values), consistent with trials 1–128, but the spacing is now physically plausible (~0.003–0.08 beat units) rather than suspiciously quantized. I must immediately: (1) examine the data-collection and processing logs for trials 131–139 to determine whether the logging regime changed again or was corrected; (2) re-examine trials 1–128 for evidence of deduplication or rounding that may have been retroactively applied or logged; (3) reconsider whether the fine spacing and zero-repetition count reflect genuine measurement precision under some data-handling rule I have not yet identified. The level shift in post-baseline vs baseline (z≈18.48) remains, but is now less clearly attributable to logging regime change if the recent trials show normal variance. I must audit the pipeline immediately and revise the hypothesis set to reflect the new evidence structure.

Day 36 continuation of post-baseline phase measurement series.
